script.title: Why Ships Waited Forty Days Before Entering Venice

lines: A ship full of sailors had to wait forty days before going ashore.
The reason was the Black Death.
Between 1348 and 1359, the plague killed an estimated 30% of Europe's people.
Venice acted first. In 1348, it named three guardians of public health.
In 1377, the city of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, made newcomers wait thirty days.
They waited on nearby islands, to see if plague symptoms appeared.
Then in 1403, Venice opened a plague hospital on a small island beside the city.
In 1448, the Venetian Senate stretched the wait to forty days.
In Venetian, that period was called quarantena.
It's where our word quarantine comes from.
You see, it's like bumping your knee.
You wait a day to see if a bruise shows up.
Today's estimates say plague took 37 days from infection to death.
So forty days was long enough to show who carried it.
The forty-day rule proved an effective way to handle outbreaks.
But the number forty may not have come from doctors counting days.
Scholars link it to the medicine of Hippocrates and the forty days of Lent.

claims.claim: Ships were required to be isolated before passengers and crew could go ashore during the Black Death; quarantena means forty days.
Between 1348 and 1359 the Black Death wiped out an estimated 30% of Europe's population.
Venice appointed three guardians of public health in the first years of the Black Death (1348).
In 1377 Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik) made newcomers spend 30 days, originally on nearby islands, to see whether Black Death symptoms developed.
Venice founded the first lazaret, on a small island adjoining the city, in 1403.
In 1448 the Venetian Senate prolonged the waiting period to 40 days, giving birth to the term quarantine.
Current estimates give bubonic plague a 37-day period from infection to death; the forty-day quarantine proved an effective formula for handling outbreaks.
The 40 days has a strong association with the medical theory of Hippocrates and the Lenten season.
